# Physical diagnosis (percussion, stethoscope, thermometer, pulse count) (`clinical_thermometer_stethoscope`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by thermometer_temperature, anatomy_dissection, mechanical_clock, data_graphs
- Core idea: Examine the body instead of only questioning the patient and looking at urine. Tap the chest with a finger: air-filled lung sounds hollow like an empty cask, fluid or solid lung sounds dull. Listen through a wooden tube about 30 cm long with one end on the chest and the other at the ear: breathing, crackles and heart sounds are heard clearly and differ in pneumonia, consumption and heart disease. Count the pulse against a watch (60–100 a minute at rest in an adult) and the breaths (12–20). Measure the temperature with a small mercury thermometer under the tongue or in the armpit for several minutes (normal about 37 °C, within half a degree) and plot it twice daily; the curve tracks the illness but usually cannot identify its cause. Each sign means something in the context of symptoms, other findings and the course of illness. Comparing bedside findings with autopsies helped establish those associations.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting the instrument to cure; it only tells diseases apart
  - Treating fever as the disease itself and fighting the number
  - Thinking the stethoscope amplifies; it mainly isolates the sound, and an untrained ear hears nothing useful
  - Using a room thermometer that responds slowly and is read after removal, when it has already fallen
  - Quoting 37.0 °C as exact; healthy people vary by time of day
- History: egypt: c. 300 BC – Herophilus of Alexandria times the pulse with a water clock; china: c. 280 – Wang Shuhe's Mai jing systematises pulse diagnosis; europe: c. 1612 – Santorio uses a thermoscope on patients; 1707 Floyer's pulse watch; 1761 Auenbrugger (Vienna) describes percussion; 1816–1819 Laennec invents the stethoscope; 1867 Allbutt's short clinical thermometer; 1868 Wunderlich's fever curves from about 25,000 patients; 1896 Riva-Rocci's blood-pressure cuff
- Read:
  - René Laennec, De l'auscultation médiate (1819)
  - Carl Wunderlich, Das Verhalten der Eigenwärme in Krankheiten (1868)
  - Stanley Joel Reiser, Medicine and the Reign of Technology (1978)
